question:
Patient note:
A 27-year-old woman sits cross-legged on the stretcher in the ambulatory sports-medicine suite while the orthopedic resident completes consent for a planned left shoulder arthroscopy with labral debridement; the attending expects scope time of roughly forty minutes under general anesthesia with discharge early this evening. She arrived from home on foot after a short rideshare, wheeled her own overnight bag, and jokes that she “can still out-pace the interns on the stairs,” illustrating that her daily activity remains unrestricted—she attends yoga classes, cycles to her graduate lectures, and sleeps on a standard flat pillow without orthopnea. The shoulder injury occurred during an indoor rock-climbing fall two months ago, and since then she has used only a soft sling intermittently for comfort; there has been no casting, splinting, traction, or enforced immobilization of any limb, and she continues to type term papers without difficulty. Review of recent events, however, reveals that three weeks before today she spent four days on a medical ward for a community-acquired multilobar pneumonia that presented with fever to 39 °C, productive cough, and an oxygen saturation nadir of 90 % on room air; blood cultures stayed negative, chest radiograph showed right lower-lobe consolidation, and she improved rapidly after ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Because the admitting team anticipated a prolonged oral-intolerance phase, a single-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter was placed in the right basilic vein for intravenous therapy; that line remains in situ now, secured with a clear occlusive dressing, flushing easily, and the nursing record shows brisk sanguineous return without erythema or tenderness along the arm. She has not undergone any other operation, endoscopic intervention, or radiologic procedure in the thirty days preceding today, and the electronic chart is free of heart-failure admissions, urosepsis, or catheter-associated bacteremia entries. Past medical history is otherwise limited to childhood appendectomy and a biochemical work-up last year for episodic migraine that disclosed mildly raised fasting homocysteine at 18 µmol/L; she was advised to take daily folate and B-complex vitamins, which she does regularly. She denies chronic lung disease, connective-tissue disorder, inflammatory bowel symptoms, malignancy, myocardial ischemia, or episodes of transient neurologic deficit. She has never experienced calf swelling, pleuritic chest discomfort, or radiologically confirmed clot, and she has not been exposed to heparin products except for standard peri-catheter flushes, which have caused no platelet count drop. When asked about relatives, she recalls that her father required six months of anticoagulation for a lower-extremity thrombosis after a long-haul flight in his early forties, and a paternal aunt had an “unexplained lung clot” after minor gynecologic surgery, prompting her primary physician to counsel vigilance during future hospitalizations. Medications this morning include ibuprofen 400 mg taken with a sip of water for shoulder soreness, combined ethinyl-estradiol/levonorgestrel oral contraceptive paused four days ago per surgeon instruction, and the aforementioned vitamins; she does not take glucocorticoids, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs. She has never smoked, enjoys one glass of red wine on weekends, denies recreational substances, and maintains a body mass index of 23 kg/m² on a plant-forward diet. Physical examination performed twenty minutes ago finds her alert, conversational, and afebrile at 36.8 °C; blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats min⁻¹ and regular, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class I with full cervical range, intact dentition, and thyromental distance of three fingerbreadths. Jugular venous contour lies below the clavicle with the head elevated to 30°, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and peripheral pulses are bounding and symmetric. Auscultation of the lungs demonstrates clear breath sounds bilaterally with no residual crackles or wheeze. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender; surgical scars are confined to a well-healed right lower-quadrant appendectomy incision. Inspection of the extremities shows no varicosities, edema, or cord-like structures, and calf circumferences measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity are equal at 34 cm. The right basilic line is noted just above the antecubital fossa under a transparent film with no erythema or drainage, and there are no additional vascular devices. Neurologic screening yields intact cranial nerves and 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups except for mild pain-limited external rotation in the injured shoulder. Laboratory studies collected via the catheter at 06:00 demonstrate hemoglobin 13.8 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 41 %, leukocytes 6.4 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelets 256 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 140 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 23 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.78 mg dL⁻¹, AST 19 U L⁻¹, ALT 21 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 11.9 s with international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. A screening electrocardiogram reviewed by anesthesia shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats min⁻¹, normal intervals, and no repolarization abnormalities, while the posterior-anterior chest radiograph obtained during the pneumonia admission, re-examined today, shows resolving right lower-lobe infiltrate with normal cardiac silhouette and catheter tip terminating in the distal superior vena cava. She has remained nil per os since midnight, pneumatic compression sleeves are wrapped around both calves but not yet activated, and no chemoprophylactic anticoagulant has been administered as the team awaits induction of anesthesia.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE risk score sums weighted perioperative risk factors. Using the Caprini version that lists arthroscopic surgery as a 2-point procedure:
- Planned shoulder arthroscopy → 2. Do not also score it as minor surgery.
- Pneumonia within the past month (3 weeks ago) → 1.
- Central venous access (PICC still in place) → 2.
- Family history of VTE (father with DVT and aunt with PE) → 3, counted once.
- Elevated homocysteine (18 µmol/L) → 3.
Age 27 and BMI 23 add no points. No qualifying bed rest, cast, personal VTE, or malignancy is documented. The combined contraceptive was stopped before assessment and is not counted as current therapy.
Sum: 2 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 11.
Final answer: 11
